This study examines the generalization performance of two-layer neural networks applied to determining the ground state of the Schr\"odinger operator within a $d$-dimensional hypercube framework. Under the assumption that the ground state resides in a spectral Barron space, the authors establish that the convergence of the generalization error remains decaying at a rate independent of dimensionality. It is assumed throughout that the input features are uniformly distributed, and the investigation covers an arbitrary finite horizon. The theoretical findings are bolstered by numerical experiments.

This study analyzes the largest dataset to date from the Pierre Auger Observatory, encompassing 530 ultra-high-energy cosmic rays detected above 4 EeV. A consistent trend has been identified within the energy spectrum exceeding 8 EeV, suggesting an anisotropic distribution and a preference for sources in the southern celestial hemisphere, particularly around longitudes near -40°. Given that this signal aligns with an excess of ultra-high-energy events recorded between 8.2 and 8.4 EeV during the initial operational phase of the observatory, a potential instrumental bias linked to seasonal detector calibration is being examined as a competing explanation.

We demonstrate the presence of global in time solutions within the Friedrichs part of the spin-1/2 particle semilinear equation theory, specifically for potentials exhibiting a growth rate between cubic and linear. This existence relies on implementing the Lochak-Majorana condition on the linear term of two spinors, which notably permits theories with subquadratic potential energy. These findings rely primarily on suitable norm estimates of the two spinors involved and their propagators, alongside spectral properties of the operator governing said spinors. These results extend prior work by O. Piret regarding equations involving the standard Dirac operator.

Federated learning represents a promising approach for harnessing widely dispersed data sources to train deep learning models while ensuring privacy by preventing raw data from leaving local environments. This study explores the application of federated learning in analyzing whole slide histopathology images. The method involved collaborative training of models to detect malign cells across 23 institutions in the UK and France. Despite challenges related to batch effect variations between batches and countries, the proposed method of locally training convolutional neural networks (CNNs) proved viable. Furthermore, it yielded generalizable models that rival those trained on aggregated centralised data. The findings suggest that federated learning can successfully support multi-institutional collaborations in medical image analysis while safeguarding patient confidentiality.

Cavity magnomechanics offers an excellent platform for investigating macroscopic quantum phenomena by integrating magnons, phonons, and photons within one system. The development of cavity magnomechanical configurations that provide clean nonlinear coupling between these three entities has significantly enriched quantum physics research. In this study, we demonstrate that a surface acoustic wave (SAW)-driven cavity magnomechanical system rooted on yttrium iron garnet thin films supports distinct triple and six-two wave mixing interactions. These coupling mechanisms facilitate various nonlinear effects, including single and composite phonon Fock state generation, as well as cavity magnon and mechanical coherent states. Given the growing significance of such multi-mode interactions in quantum physics, this work lays a practical groundwork for advanced applications, such as three-mode quantum entanglement and quantum information manipulation.

This paper reveals a revolutionary reinforcement learning (RL)-based solution for quadrupedal walking, featuring an evolutionary trajectory optimizer that dynamically adapts to terrain. Traditionally, applying RL directly within the control loop to learn footpaths has been hindered by extremely slow training convergence. We address this limitation with a new methodology that evolves trajectories outside the simulation in multiple iterations, optimizing for terminal velocity upon contact to ensure successful stance landings. Guided by real-time feedback from this optimization process, the primary RL policy refines its control strategy, learning to manipulate the robot for successful locomotion. We have implemented this technique on RaHling, our real physical bot. Experimental comparisons highlight that our approach surpasses prior trajectory methods in learning efficiency and convergence speed. Notably, after just 250 physical simulations seconds, the robot developed a stable gait capable of executing controlled steps.

Lags of active galactic nuclei (LAGNs) are defined as systems where the accretion rate falls below $\sim10^{-3}$ of their Eddington limit. Despite their prevalence, observing the accretion process within LAGNs remains challenging. This study employs novel, high-resolution, full-spectrum relativistic magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulations to investigate the spectral energy distribution (SED) of both LAGNs and highly luminous active galactic nuclei (LAGNs) across a broad spectrum of black hole masses and accretion rates. The study successfully reproduces the observed spectral energy distribution of LAGNs, notably including those with masses around $10^6$ solar radii. The model accurately reproduces the power-law spectral energy distribution of LAGNs, notably including those of $6$ critical point self-similar solutions in four-dimensional full-relativistic magnetohydrodynamic simulations to explore spectral energy distribution of low-accretion-rate active galactic nuclei.

This paper introduces a data-driven redesign approach for nonlinear controllers within closed-loop systems utilizing reinforcement learning (RL). Since traditional RL methods applied to control redesign can demand excessive simulation steps and often lack guaranteed convergence to an optimal policy, we leverage existing closed-loop data generated by current controllers to accelerate the learning process through the implementation of relative states. Our methodology leverages relative states to incorporate historical trajectory information, facilitating more rapid policy optimization targeted at improving controller performance. Furthermore, we incorporate barrier functions to guarantee safe exploration during the update phases. Simulation studies on relative navigation tasks for spacecraft demonstrate that incorporating relative states significantly accelers the reinforcement learning convergence compared to standard methods.

The SiD Tracker represents a key detection apparatus intended for the international SLAC Belle II experiment, featuring a resolution for charged particle momentum ($1/\sqrt{p_t}$) of outstanding precision. This design incorporates a dense arrangement of silicon sensors with thin active layers, silicon carbide (SiC) substrates, positioned closely around the primary interaction site. Complemented by a substantial external drift chamber operating with multi-parameter space reconstruction (MPSR), the SiD Tracker enables robust identification and precise measurement of final-state particles produced from $\tau$-lepton decays as well as from prompt and delayed vertexing related to neutral strands.

Monitoring the state of the Earth is vital for addressing global environmental and social challenges, from managing forests and cities to mitigating climate change impacts. Today, various sensor types capture vast Earth observation (EO) data sets, enabling global monitoring initiatives like Copernicus. These data include multiple satellite imagery sources alongside data on land, air, and the ocean. However, managing this complex, multi-sensor information remains difficult due to data redundancy arising from similar acquisitions. While traditional methods struggle with such complexities, recent studies indicate that AI algorithms can effectively model these scenarios, though they require extensive testing. This paper introduces new approaches to AI utilization within the copious multi-sensor Earth observation realm. We present two specific solutions: first, a method for pinpointing neglected or overlooked satellite image acquisitions, and second, predictive models for one satellite type derived from others. Ultimately, we demonstrate how Artificial Intelligence can streamline EO dataset administration, aiding planners in aligning AI research with administration needs.

Furthermore, these methods demand extensive archives of past records and incur substantial storage and computational costs. This paper presents NEWAD, a novel self-supervised deep learning approach designed to identify spatio-temporal anomalies using only real-time sensor data. NEWAD utilizes a self-supervised strategy that extracts comprehensive complementary features through two specialized modules: an Explorative module that locates and analyzes local exceptionalities, and a Utilitarian module that maps global exceptionalities. Additionally, robust resilience tests indicate NEWAD performs optimally under uncertain conditions. Finally, a thorough investigation into decision uncertainties reveals insightful anamoly characteristics inherent in urban mobility systems.

Since interpreting code's functionality constitutes both code comprehension and program analysis, various graph-based models have been proposed by leveraging the inherent structural connections within programming sources. However, these approaches often neglect semantic aspects of the problems for which the code serves as a solution. Our research introduces "code as graph," where graph nodes encapsade comprehensive semantic information derived from the solution context. Through an examination of over 350,000 functions across 3 distinct domains—namely SQuAD and two additional large-scale code datasets—we identified the prevalent entity types present in the data. Our method offers several innovative contributions: a novel dataset featuring annotated function descriptions, sophisticated semantic parsing capabilities including the extraction of Python code directly from natural language, and in-depth analytics on code structure and semantics.

We determine the stellar-to-halo mass relation (SHMR) for early-type galaxies (ETGs) utilizing an independent sample located in the Sun's neighborhood, distinct from those used to calibrate the mass function. By fitting cold dark matter simulations with a phenomenological model derived from this new sample, we identify a consistent SHMR featuring significant asymmetry, peaking at a halo mass of $10^{11} M_\odot$. While early peak ETG ratios reach $0.6 M_\odot$ (approximately double the values of late-type galaxies), the ratio declines steeply for masses exceeding $1.5 \times 10^{11} M_\odot$ and slowly for earlier masses. Additionally, we quantify an inherent asymmetry in SHMR evolution across all redshifts, finding that late-type galaxies exhibit higher stellar-to-halo mass ratios at lower redshifts. Finally, we examine potential biases in SHMR determinations by comparing these independent results with original measurements; we find early-type galaxies in the central regions exceed those in outskirts by 15–30%, whereas previously used phenomenological models underestimate this difference by a factor of 2–3.

This study introduces a technique to mitigate the impact of variable stellar point spread functions (PSFs) on the vertical aerosol optical depth measurements derived from stellar photometry. The approach utilizes a subset of images from the same dataset, employing PSFs derived from these same images to restore the non-PSU corrected images. The final performance metric is represented as a function of the fraction employed for this purpose to achieve normalization. The technique is demonstrated using data from the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) and the Large Synoptic Survey Telescope (LSST), although it applies more broadly. The results demonstrate that for a given dataset, increasing the portion allocated to PSF correction leads to higher precision in the resulting aerosol optical depth values, achieving approximately a factor of improvement when allocating up to a substantial proportion. The study concludes that allocating around 30% of a dataset to this correction yields a precision sufficient for climate studies, specifically reaching less than 10% uncertainty in the vertical aerosol optical depth. The study also indicates that this approach is particularly beneficial when dealing with datasets containing fewer frames, such as those with only 10% of the volume required for traditional calibration.

In contrast, with regard to the locally low-rank property, we employ local Graphons to offer a nonparametric methodology. The proposed LiGGLA model is solved algorithmically using updated estimators for both local Graphons and sparse precision matrices by means of localized update rules. For the purpose estimating parameters and inferring the structure, we provide consistent estimators based on this solution approach. Additionally, we apply cross-validation techniques to assist in selecting the optimal cliques for graph partitioning and explain the selection process of optimal cliades for partitioning selected cliades based on some heuristics through cross-validation methods. Finally, we apply the LiGGLA model to a variety of synthetic data and real world examples to demonstrate how well it works in these cases and its performance on real world applications.

This study utilizes 1.3 mm ALMA observations of gas in the disk of TW Hydrae to analyze the photoevaporation-driven wind. We detect a redward-peaked emission profile extending outward from the disk, a structure well-modeled by photoevaporation following Nakamoto & Nakagawa (1997) that locates a minimum photoionization radius at approximately 16–17 AU. This result places GW and GT-type photoionizing winds driven by stellar UV as the leading explanations for similar phenomena in other systems, such as AB Auriga and SOJ 100. Comparing models with observations determines that a photoionization lifetime of 100 years is preferred, yielding a mass loss rate of about $10^{-10}$ solar masses per year driven internally. However, feasible mass losses can also arise externally through photoionization mechanisms operating with lifetime parameters between 10 and 100 years.

Detecting voiced speech, estimating the fundamental frequency, and continuously tracking harmonic structure are vital components of crucial techniques such as voiced speech detection and pitch tracking. While several algorithms address the entire pipeline—from automatic voiced detection through robust pitch tracking to reliable formant estimation—we focus here on an advanced algorithm for formant estimation. To achieve this, we present a new method for automatically identifying the spectrum model order and selecting the most appropriate track-and-trace algorithm. Additionally, we introduce a unified framework for automatic algorithm selection that relies on analyzing power spectrum characteristics within specific time windows. Field-tested algorithms include a frequency-domain approach featuring adaptive formant tracking alongside a novel hybrid model combining elements of both time-domain and frequency-domain techniques.

We introduce a new Dynamically Weighted Inertial Forward-Backward (DWIFOB) algorithm designed to address structured monotone inclusion problems. We further derive a specific set of parameters suitable for nearly all practical applications. Consequently, this algorithm finds use in various image processing domains, including denoising, deconvolution, and face recognition.

Recent years have seen neural architecture search (NAS) emerge as a powerful technique for automatically generating superior neural network models. However, current dominant methods remain confined to basic, simplistic search spaces that prioritize rapid initial performance gains. These approaches, despite their utility, fail to explore the vast design landscape of modern neural networks. We introduce Space of Abstract Connections (SAC), an extensive yet learnable abstract architecture defined by multi-layer subgraph structures. Our work presents PEACEN, a neural algorithm capable of directly predicting safe and high-efficiency graph topologies within the SAC framework. Empirical evaluations indicate that PEACEN can effectively generate models rivaling those manually crafted by human experts, achieving comparable accuracy and efficiency. In contrast, standard automatic weight tuning and existing end-to-end methods yield suboptimal outcomes, either lagging significantly behind human designs or failing to fully capitalize on SAC's potential due to exploration inefficiencies. Furthermore, our method demonstrates notable performance in cross-task generalizations.

Multicast beamforming is essential for delivering data efficiently to multiple users sharing the same resource block. This study addresses multicast beamforming design for orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) systems, aiming to maximize total spectral efficiency (SE) across all active users transmitted on a specific subcarrier. To achieve precise data transmission, the problem first identifies the optimal active user subset before optimizing the multicast beamforming vectors accordingly. The resulting formulation, cast as a mixed-integer non-convex optimization problem, is decomposed into two sequential subproblems: one concerning user selection and the other concerning beamforming design. These subproblems are solved alternately; the user selection task is solved through a greedy approach, while the beamforming design employs the Converged Sequential Approach. Both methodologies are implemented within an iterative framework to find problem solutions. Convergence of the proposed algorithm is demonstrated, and the performance of the suggested method is evaluated against standard benchmarks, comparing total SE and individual downlink SE for various active user subsets. Furthermore, the impact of simulation parameters on performance is analyzed and discussed.

Communication efficiency is a critical factor for enabling Federated Learning (FL), a decentralized machine learning approach that protects user data privacy by avoiding its direct sharing. This paper proposes a newly optimized framework called Federated Distillation (FD) to enhance FL communication efficiency. Unlike standard FL, which necessitates frequent model parameter updates from participating clients, FD transmits only local predictions generated at each end-device. By doing so, FD achieves substantial communication savings—potentially as high as $N$ times better than FL, where $N$ represents the number of clients. This capability makes FD an ideal solution for large-scale deployments. We analyze the theoretical implications of applying an error-accumulation-based distortion control strategy and a regularization term to ensure model consistency. Experimental results across multiple datasets and with various client selection policies indicate that FD reduces communication costs by an order of magnitude compared to FL, while delivering competitive accuracy relative to FL and other leading distillation techniques.

Named Data Networking (NDN) represents a promising architecture for evolving distributed computing networks, offering enhanced data security, privacy, and reliability while supporting data-centric applications. This paper presents an experimental evaluation of NDN-based file sharing, focusing on systems with random request patterns and the impact of concurrent requests on common services like Wikipedia, YouTube, Twitter, and Google. Our results indicate that concurrent access significantly boosts system throughput and reduces latency. Furthermore, our study outlines ongoing research priorities regarding load balancing, caching strategies, and routing protocols within NDN environments.

Current multi-objective optimization approaches typically rely on a fixed utility function or interact with experts through preference-based queries. However, predefined functions are difficult to formulate for complex, conflicting goals, and expert interaction imposes significant latency, resulting in slow systems. To address this, we introduce *learned query optimization*, a preference-free framework where the optimizer directly estimates a utility function from data using a learned function. This method enables rapid optimization responses, eliminates the need for expert preference queries, and formally extends preference learning within interactive optimization environments. Our approach elegantly unifies multiple domains, specifically multi-objective optimization, bandit problems, and preference learning. We further generalize traditional bandit mechanisms by enabling general policy learning across arbitrary objectives, rather than restricting themselves to action rewards. Evaluation across simulations, real-world datasets, and actual experiments demonstrates both high efficiency and superior performance.

Our results indicate that even minimal perturbations applied to observations can completely neutralize an agent's planning capabilities.

Validated through real-world experiments using three open-source ITS platforms, our findings demonstrate that the DITS protocol successfully performs privacy-preserving transfers while maintaining efficiency, achieving an average processing time under two seconds.

Current numerical methods for solving continuous-time dynamic optimization problems in the model predictive control (MPC) framework focus on cases where closed-form analytical optimizations exist; for scenarios lacking analytical solutions, these approaches resort to generic, black-box, derivative-free optimization algorithms. Derivative-based numerical differentiation is typically employed to obtain gradients and Jacobians within differential algebraic equation systems, yet this can yield inaccurate results due to finite step-size limitations, leading to poor optimizer performance. Moreover, deriving gradients via symbolic differentiation is often impractical due to the excessive computational complexity and memory requirements of digital platforms. Addressing this, machine learning techniques have enabled the training of neural differential solvers that yield exact analytical derivatives for dynamic optimization problems. Leveraging this capability, this work introduces an MPC scheme utilizing Neural Differential Solvers (NDS) for derivative-based optimization. Experimental comparisons demonstrate that this proposed method is more efficient and efficient than standard explicit finite-difference gradient estimation.

A rational function $f$ defined over the extended complex plane $\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$ with precisely two critical points corresponds, under its natural conformal structure, to a holomorphic self-map of degree $d$ that exhibits exactly two multiple fibers. By employing a novel approach grounded in $\overline{M}_1\overline{S}_1$ hybrid system characteristics, we analyze the decay channels $J/\psi\omega$ and $e^+e^-$ for the $Y(4230)$ resonance. Our calculations reveal that the $e^+e^-$ branching fraction aligns well with existing experimental data; furthermore, we propose that the $Y(4230)$ exhibits a pronounced peak in the $\overline{M}_1\overline{M}_1$ mode. These findings offer promising prospects for further investigations into the $Y(4230)$ using the BESSII detector.

This study introduces three distinct methods for quantifying the attributes of online signature templates, specifically targeting distinctiveness, complexity, and repeatability. The measure for distinctiveness is determined from a collection of enrolled signature samples alongside assumptions regarding the randomness of unrelated signs. Complexity is calculated using a model based on Markov chains, utilizing transitions derived from a single template. Repeatability assesses how consistent a user's signatures remain under the assumption of randomness for unrelated individuals, evaluated using the same markovian complexity model. Enrolled templates are categorized according to these metrics, allowing for a balance in selecting signs that are sufficiently unique and complex while maintaining acceptable variation. The utility of this three-measure framework in selecting online signatures is validated through experiments.

This manuscript investigates the perturbative spectrum of massless bosonic fields in ten-dimensional type II T-fold backgrounds, which exhibit N=6 supersymmetry, within the framework of O(D+1,D+1)/Z(4)(D+1,D+1)/Z(4)-T-duality. We examine two specific examples, analyzing how massless bosonic fields organize themselves within representations of specific symmetric groups. Our analysis reveals that these supersymmetries perturbation theories behave differently under 1-loop corrections, suggesting that their nonperturbative behaviors might be equivalent. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for a particular set of examples, deriving D-tail the duals of these theories by applying O(D+1,D+1)/Z(4) T-duality transformations. Finally, we explore whether these perturbative theories share nonperturbative behaviors despite their differing 1-loop corrections.

We examine the magnetic dressing of one dopant within the one-half-filled Hubbard model, emphasizing how its motion influences the system's properties. In the metallic phase, phonon-mimicked dressing exhibits greater metallic character, whereas in the Mott insulating state, the dressing remains largely hubb-bond-like and spatially confined. We suggest that simulating this doping behavior with a bosonic-flux-carrying impurity could effectively reproduce the observed magnetic dressing effects.

Secondary nitrogen enrichment is prominent in massive and AGB stars within the 4–6 k$_{\odot}$ range; however, AGB contributions are limited to low metallicities. Using a mixing length theory framework with radial overshoot, our modeling demonstrates that the extent of overshoot dictates stellar mass loss—a factor critical for identifying the core mass of AGB stars through core mass loss laws. Our findings indicate a unique mass ejection regime triggered by internal mixing in stars exceeding 4 k$_{\odot}$. This regime creates a core mass loss relationship with distinct ejection parameters separate from those applicable to smaller massive stars. Furthermore, the second phase of nitrogen production occurs via carbon burning and transformation into nitrogen within hydrogen-burning shells of asymptotic giant branch stars, involving the second-hybridization shell blue flash. This process generates secondary nitrogen in high-mass stars above 4 k$_{\odot}$ but remains unfeasible in lower-mass stars beneath that threshold.

Biomedical data are frequently expressed as graphs, a format that enables graph neural networks to excel in machine learning for medicine and healthcare. Over the last ten years, substantial progress has been made in developing methods for representing graphs. This review examines key advances in graph-based biomedicine machine learning, outlines significant case studies, and identifies future opportunities within this dynamic field.

We present an analysis of luminosity data from solar-white-dwarf systems within our galaxy, exploring potential impacts from WIMP annihilation on their cores. Our findings reveal that, absent a strongly suppressed interaction cross-section, WIMPs would typically penetrate these stars and reach white dwarfs (and neutron stars) following a collisionless trajectory. Accumulation of such particles in the compact cores generates an energy influx that could sustain observed luminosity through dwarf-star heating and subsequent cooling. We detail expected signatures resulting from this WIMP-induced opacity effect. Notably, if such particles exist in significant quantities, the luminosity of a white dwarf would fall more gradually than currently predicted by standard stellar evolution models. We find that current data from COSBAY satellites provide constraints on both cosmic acceleration mechanisms and supernova events, alongside limits imposed by absence of detectable signals.

Many individuals underestimate the privacy risks associated with uploading photos to the internet. This paper introduces the Graph Privacy Advisor, an application that acts as an image privacy classifier. It predicts privacy status by analyzing scene details and the number of objects present. To achieve greater accuracy, the system incorporates specific scene context through an intermediate object classifier. Objects are identified using a state-of-the-art detector, with subsequent counts facilitated by majority-voting mechanisms. These data points—object counts and scene classifications—serve as inputs for a graph-based classifier tailored to estimate the probability that an image is private. To validate the approach, a novel dataset containing approximately 30,000 images was compiled, split into roughly 25,000 images for in-phase testing and 100 images reserved for out-of-phase testing to ensure robustness. Empirical results indicate the method achieves high accuracy on the in-phase set (91.8%) and maintains strong performance on unseen data from the out-of-phase set (83.3%).

Solar atmospheric observations reveal vast networks of magnetic fields anchored to the photosphere, supporting coronal loops heated to temperatures exceeding 1 million Kelvin. Nanoflares, small-scale magnetic reconnection events, are proposed as the primary heating mechanism for these loops. By modeling nanoflare dynamics, we can determine if they exhibit self-polarity, a property where energy release scales with magnetic structure, implying significant stability. This work presents a theoretical framework for self-polarity within nanoflares, linking it to broader concepts such as wave power and coronal heating as well as radiation stability issues. By integrating observations with mathematical models of loop heating and radiative loss functions, we demonstrate a clear path forward for investigating the self-polarity hypothesis regarding nanoflares.

Data augmentation is an established technique in machine learning that enhances performance by introducing varied training samples; however, its application in graph neural networks for predicting social influence remains unexplored. This paper introduces novel methods to augment graph data specifically tailored for social influence forecasting. We assess four distinct augmentation strategies on the augmented CLIC dataset alongside large-scale real-world social graphs, analyzing how variations in structure and sampling influence model outputs. Results demonstrate that augmenting via multiple walk sampling consistently improves social influence model accuracy and provides robustness against noise. Furthermore, the proposed approaches deliver significant improvements on real-world datasets, outperforming baseline models, and show particularly strong efficacy on the expansive CLIC dataset.

This research addresses pose estimation using general point-set methodologies, specifically evaluating how dataset characteristics influence performance limits. We derive the error covariance matrix based on natural point-set inversion and determine the Cramér-Rao lower bound for estimator performance, ultimately proposing an approach for estimating how control variables affect pose estimation precision. Applied to set registration, this framework calculates precision gains achievable through points constrained in position or location uncertainty. Furthermore, the study introduces a fundamental relationship linking pose estimation to minimum nuclear norm estimators.

Various models rooted in string theory and supergravity feature hidden sectors that hold significant cosmological and particle physics implications, including dark matter, mass hierarchies, inflation in the early universe, and electroweak symmetry breaking. This paper explores how cosmological phenomena within these hidden sectors might reveal themselves through modern particle physics experiments and Higgs decays associated with electroweak inflation in the nascent stages of cosmic evolution.

This paper details the inaugural observation of same-sign W boson pair production in proton-proton collisions at $\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV, utilizing recorded data from the CMS experiment at the CERN LHC with an integrated luminosity of 35.9 fb$^{-1}$. The analysis targets final states containing exactly four charged leptons (electrons or muons) and eight jets. A significant event signature arises from at least seven jets carrying a high transverse momentum ($p_{\mathrm{T}} > 30$ GeV). Selection criteria filter for a specific kinematic topology featuring two "recoil" substructures, each containing a same-sign W boson pair, alongside four jet-repair events. Following rigorous background estimation and fitting of the diboson mass spectrum, a statistically significant excess is identified. This finding aligns with Standard Model forecasts for WW production. Furthermore, signals of potential physics beyond the Standard Model are constrained by comparing observed yields against theoretical predictions.

This paper proposes an end-to-end deep learning framework for the co-learning of monochrome and color image super-resolution, a system designed and tested specifically for OLIMPUS's OL2000 model camera that features colors-and-mono dual-lens configuration. Since some OL2000 models come with built-in monochrome filters, this approach enables OL2000 to achieve superior results by integrating the monochrome information into the color image restoration processes. Furthermore, since human vision relies more on chromatic details than clarity, this method enhances visual quality in OL2000 images using their lower-res color data. The mathematical relationship between these two types of cameras forms our training objective, which is then solved by training two separate networks side-by-side to improve efficiency.

We investigate two recently proposed extensions involving the lensing consistency parameter, $A_L$, within the $\Lambda$CDM framework using lensing and $\kappa\theta$ statistics from the Planck 2018 data. Without any $A_L$ correction, these observational datasets appear inconsistent with the Hubble tension; incorporating $A_L$ offers an alternative pathway to address this discrepancy. Specifically, we evaluate two distinct implementations: first, a multiplicative factor applied to the lensing potential, and second, a "smearing" effect on the CMB angular power spectrum. Our findings reveal that both approaches yield improved statistical fit quality when lensing and $\kappa\theta$ data are included and allow the CMB power spectrum to align better with the Hubble tension. Notably we find that only the first approach—a modification to the lensing potential—successfully reconciles all Planck 2018 data with the Hubble tension, permitting $A_L$ values around 0.97$\pm$0.02. This result implies a slightly smaller size for the sound horizon.

Over the counter, over a decade has passed since meta-maintenance emerged as a novel approach to reframing software development challenges, shifting the focus toward managing variability and ambiguity within requirement changes. This article provides a comprehensive survey of existing research related to meta-maintenance, documenting various associated concepts, definitions, motivations, and methodologies. In addition to outlining current challenges, we suggest several promising research avenues rooted in this novel paradigm.

Combining these observations with astrometry from various sources allows for the derivation of the binary star BD And mass, radius, and luminosity. Comparatively, the primary binary star BD And cannot expand further based on the fact that it is a main-sequence dwarf star. Through modeling ejections, the binary star BD And cannot absorb more mass in order to expand. We hypothesize mass transfer or stellar wind mass ejections. Cross-domain recommendation models aim to enhance prediction accuracy by leveraging auxiliary information from related datasets; yet, existing approaches often rely on assuming data are fully observable or ignore sparse issues within the source domain. This study introduces Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR), which effectively handles scenarios involving both significant sparsity in target and source data. MSDCR achieves this by integrating multiple source datasets and minimally exploiting information from them—specifically the other's latent representations—to fill target domain gaps. The model operates in two phases: initially, it constructs a target domain autoencoder and a source domain classifier utilizing only self-data; subsequently, it co-trains these models across domains using a constructed combined objective function. Empirical results confirm that MSDCR substantially improves upon single-domain models and current cross-domain techniques, particularly in handling data scarcity across different domains.

We establish that for any smooth projective scheme, the vector space capturing the first-order variations of a sheaf equipped with either an orthogonal (respectively symplectic) structure corresponds exactly to the first hyper-cohomology of a specific, derived complex intrinsically associated to that structure. Additionally, we present the corresponding obstruction theory for such sheaves, which is governed by an obstruction theory based on second cohomology of this same complex, as well as one based on standard cohomology ($\text{coh}^2$) for locally free resolutions.

We examine strategies for approximating functions within reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHS) that are derived from noisy data. We establish $l_2$-risk bounds for this estimation process and delineate aspects of the bias-variance trade-off specific to the chosen approximation method. These findings consider two distinct selection approaches: fixing the approximation subspace dimension or selecting its dimension based on validation error. Our analysis demonstrates an interest in this trade-off regarding sample size and space dimensionality. Specifically, validating error-based selection shows that even when accounting for noisy samples, dividing by the square root of subspace dimension yields optimal risk convergence by balancing bias and variance, provided no noise exists. Additionally, assuming noise-free samples and smooth target functions relative to the kernel, we prove that this dimension-balanced strategy significantly reduces risk more favorably than methods employing fixed dimensions. Finally, we outline potential extensions for scenarios involving noisy functions on compact manifolds.

We introduced a straightforward method to calculate the transport of heavy mesons in ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions, focusing on two key parameters: yield and momentum distribution. Operating within an ideal quark-partition model, the study applies this technique specifically to $K^0_L$ electrons and $D^0$ electrons. Parameters governing $q\bar{q}$ pair creation and scattering off ultra-relativistic ions are adjusted to align with existing electron and positron collision data. The model is then used to analyze $\mu^+\mu^-$ electron and $D$ electron production during ultra-relativistic Pb-Pb collisions at 2.76 TeV. By comparing outcomes against experimental results from the CMS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider, our findings demonstrate reasonable consistency. Furthermore, we investigate the influence of various parameters on the $q\bar{q}$ creation and scattering processes governing electron production.

Detecting correlations between distant spins is crucial for verifying entanglement and for quantum computing and communication applications; furthermore, observing spin-1/2 decay, indicative of a random singlet phase, offers insights into universal critical behavior in insulators. However, this specific decay pattern has only been previously observed in superconductors. This study utilizes quantum tomography of up to 16 spins in a superconducting quantum processor to investigate entanglement in two disordered systems: one acting as an insulator and the other as a superconductor. Our findings confirm the absence of spin-1/2 decay in the insulator while simultaneously highlighting the presence of it, thereby signaling the random singlet phase. Additionally, by examining tomographic data for up to 16 spins and applying machine learning techniques, we successfully identified spin-1/2 decay more efficiently than prior methods, which required correlations on the order of 1,000 to several thousand.

Extending our analysis, we demonstrate that through appropriate parameter adjustments, this framework can simulate various topological soliton configurations typically associated with skew-field soliton theories. Specifically, we show the capacity to emulate features of vortices, domain walls, and vortex walls within the skew-field theory using solitons and coherent structures derived from the MSTB framework.

Robots employing inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) to learn from demonstrations often encounter disruptive events, such as obstacles, that necessitate corrective actions. While previous research assumes these corrections are pre-programmed and flawless, this study investigates scenarios where a human supervisor provides noisy and potentially deceptive noise. We posit that these imperfect observations constitute "noise," constituting a new category of disturbance. Our contribution includes a partial observability Markov decision process (POMDP) framework capable of accounting for imperfect human signals alongside demonstrated actions. We propose a cluster-based IRL algorithm to handle this noisy input effectively. Experiments conducted on actual robotic platforms confirm that our methodology surpasses baseline benchmark algorithms in scenarios characterized by deceptive and inconsistent human observations.

We demonstrate that every strong H-bounded one-step contraction semigroup space admits a corresponding strong SLT space via a potential covering map. However, it is also shown that certain spaces satisfy the bounded one-step contraction semigroup SLT conditions without any such metric cover existing within the strong SLT space category. Additionally, by examining specific cases of the bond metric space defined as the bounded contraction semigroup SLT type, this paper highlights instances where no effective cover exists that links this space itself to the strong SLT space.

We introduce a two-phased algorithm designed to address complex tasks within the realm of robotic control, capable of leveraging both prior knowledge and recent insights to overcome challenging control problems. Related to this, there is the development of a potential-based robotic arm strategy to handle difficult manipulation. This work focuses primarily upon creating an efficient method across two stages to improve policy. Related to this work, we develop an efficient method across two stages to refine the policy: first constructing a base strategy utilizing geometric understanding to establish effective initial conditions; secondly applying reinforcement learning to optimize this base strategy. For illustration, we present a geometric method to set up the robot state before optimization begins. This initial policy provides a strong starting foundation. Next, we optimize this base strategy using reinforcement learning techniques, demonstrating the method's efficacy through arm manipulation scenarios and simulation setups involving simulated robots performing specific control tasks.

We introduce MEGA, a new two-point statistical tool designed to identify and separate the effects of active galactic nuclei (AGN) feedback from star formation using high-resolution maps from the $E$ and $X$ power spectra. This methodology allows us to model supermassive black hole growth as well as star formation through convolution with bias and correlation functions, enabling the derivation of growth rates for black holes in the mass range of $10^6-10^9$ solar masses and stellar formation across scales from $0.1$ to $10$ parsec. By applying MEGA to simulated data generated with the IllustrativeCosmo project, we capture signal from individual black holes on small scales up to galaxy-wide properties on large scales. This enables a precise quantification of black hole growth mechanisms in high-redshift star-forming galaxies.

Deep neural networks (DL) are increasingly popular for analyzing data within CERN experiments due to their flexibility and capacity to uncover complex patterns within seemingly random datasets. Despite their potential, two significant obstacles hinder experimental scientists from leveraging this tool: a steep learning curve regarding deep methods and the computational expense of rigorous cross-validation. This study seeks to simplify DL applications within high-energy physics by demonstrating how scikit-learn can effectively model deep learning architectures. Employing this model allows researchers to balance the trade-off between development time and performance by utilizing established machine learning practices. This approach significantly simplifies model evaluation, parameter tuning, and retraining. To demonstrate this method, we employ both topological emulators and event classifiers as use cases.

Preprints represent versions of scientific manuscripts shared prior to formal journal publication, offering rapid access to findings and facilitating scholarly discussion. First established in 1967, they have historically accounted for a minor fraction of academic literature; today, they constitute approximately 1% to 5% of research articles. This study employs a large-scale dataset to evaluate the development and evolution of preprint services over the last three decades, detecting an exponential rise in their adoption. Despite three centuries of sustained growth, preprint repositories currently represent only 1% to 5% of published articles, yet their trajectory suggests a likelihood of reaching 50% within the next thirty years. Furthermore, significant disparities in development and distribution are evident across disciplines and nations, suggesting uneven global distribution. By examining these trends and variations, researchers can gain a clearer perspective on current services, identify necessary improvements, and address potential equity concerns.

Robust research data management (DDM) is crucial for the reproducibility and efficiency of data-driven deductive investigations. However, current practices within academic institutions are inadequate for these goals. We introduce Data Notebook, an electronic laboratory book specifically engineered to support researchers conducting data-driven deductive research. By facilitating the structured recording of research hypotheses, data processing workflows, and observations, Data Notebook promotes transparency and facilitates collaboration. Unlike conventional electronic lab notebooks designed for empirical research, Data Notebook is optimized for environments where researchers formulate hypotheses based on data and verify them through additional investigation.

High-entropy alloys represent a promising class of materials characterized by multi-component complexity, with machine learning methods offering robust tools for investigating their properties and guiding rational design. Nevertheless, leveraging these techniques for discovery often demands extensive experimentation that is impractical for systems involving numerous elements. To overcome this barrier, we introduce a novel data-efficient approach grounded in transfer learning and pattern association. This method constructs both conventional and descriptor-enhanced alloy clusters to establish foundational models for universal feature extraction, thereby enabling rapid discovery across diverse chemical spaces with minimal data requirements. We validate the framework using diverse datasets representing various properties of multi-component alloys, demonstrating its efficacy in guiding the identification of new high-entropy alloys. Consequently, we propose this strategy as a dependable tool for the broader material science community, capable of facilitating the universal search for high-performance alloys.

Probabilistic frameworks are fundamental to latent variable learning because they enable state estimation, which serves as an intuitive representation of the posterior distribution over hidden variables. However, conducting state estimation through sampling incurs significant computational costs that hinder its applicability in real-time applications. To overcome this limitation, this paper introduces a novel variational framework for estimating states. We derive efficient updates for the posterior distribution over hidden variables by leveraging the neural network parameters established during generative model training. Additionally, we integrate multiple regularization techniques to enhance sample quality by imposing specific structures on the posterior. Empirical evaluations across several benchmark datasets indicate that our proposed method surpasses other unsupervised state estimation techniques in terms of reconstruction score and efficiency.

The nonlinearity of a multivariational Boolean function quantifies the maximum linearity of the functions derived from varying a single variable while fixing the others. In prior research, ideas linked to Sidon sets within finite fields were utilized to establish superior nonlinearity examples with efficient designs. Nevertheless, because these earlier methods only examined even-parity functions of the form $f(x) + 1$ or $f(x)$, their results could not definitively determine the bounds for functions $f$, as the added bit alters properties when the dimension $n$ is odd. This paper extends the previously established methodology by utilizing novel Sidon sets to construct vectorial mappings with even parity. Furthermore, we analyze the geometric structure governing the lower and upper Sidon sets employed in this process. As an application, we design three distinct 11-variable functions exhibiting even parity and achieving high nonlinearity: two functions achieve a nonlinearity of 735, and one reaches 737.

Binary matrices are ubiquitous across numerous scientific and industrial domains. While structural zeros are prevalent in many of these real-world applications, they complicate the efficacy of standard sampling methods that utilize matrix-swapping techniques. This note introduces a novel row and column column-interchange strategy tailored for binary matrices incorporating structural zeros. The authors provide theoretical evidence showing that this new algorithm is ergodic, maintains consistency, and achieves asymptotically efficient results. Furthermore, extensive simulations indicate that this approach outperforms existing methods.

Achieving the fitting of Parton Distribution Function (PDFs) demands the unification of extensive datasets, drawing from both empirical observations and theoretical models. Furthermore, predicting quark and gluon distributions requires solving integro-differential equations; while an analytical solution is mathematically intractable, these equations must be numerically solved. This work updates PDF errors by merging old uncertainties with new data via a numerical method, utilizing a code developed in partnership with the LHCb collaboration.

Extending the contributions of D. Fisher and B. Tressl, we identify all integers $n \geq 1$ for which the free product of free groups $F_m * F_m$ (where the combined rank is $n$) supports a faithful, weakly mixing probability-measure-preserving action that fails to be essentially free.

Neural networks experiencing quantization often suffer degraded performance during inference, a critical challenge. This paper investigates generalized gradient descent (GGD) in quantized models where weights utilize discrete values rather than continuous real numbers. We demonstrate that even for convex objectives, gradient-based methods in such discrete settings hinder effective optimization and generalization. Specifically, we establish that learning representations becomes sample linear and theoretically impossible with finite discrete weight levels. Furthermore, considering a Bayesian perspective, we prove that using a quantized network with finite discretization yields substantially poorer out-of-distribution generalization compared to one with continuous weights. Empirical validations confirm these theoretical findings, suggesting that GGD offers negligible benefits in training quantized models. These results offer a foundational theoretical explanation for the empirically observed training difficulties in quantized neural networks.

Quantum states with a multipartite structure define a vast landscape of entropic inequalities that constrain ensemble averages of von Neumann factors. Within this framework, relative entropy dictates specific boundaries for these inequalities, distinguishing them from concepts like geometric quantization or Maurey-Embreys-Michelin theories. Using the Bulk-Boundary correspondence applicable to HRT and bulk Lego entropies—apart from violations observed in quantum gravity models where bulk entropies fail to satisfy the HEC—this work derives analogous inequality sets and explores their implications. If we assume the bulk satisfies the HEC, this assumption forces the boundary compliance and implies universal behavior across multiple subsystems. Conversely, when the bulk violates the HEC, it generates new geometric interpretations and creates potential signals for where quantum gravity theories may breach local field theories.

This paper addresses a broad class of lattice models defined on finite frameworks that generalize two previously studied categories. Like these earlier models, the conformal field theories (CFTs) linked to ours correspond directly to the lattice structures inherent in our construction. Specifically, we examine a family of such lattice-defined CFTs where the crossing multiplier for each corresponding singularity—expressed as a function of lattice geometry—is found to relate to characters of level $k$ SU(3) Wess-Zumino models. These models correspond to a set of lattice structures labeled by parameters $(p,r)$, yielding characters of the form $\chi_{a,b}(c)$. Determining which character patterns emerge requires identifying the specific conformal weights derived from the lattice construction parameters. Additionally, we explore the existence of universal crossing functions across different lattice models and estimate the dimensions of defect operators based on their connectivity within specific lattices. Finally, we explore the possibility of formulating a general theory of lattice defect lines and operator content based on defects line content.

This paper concentrates on sparse models and adaptive algorithms within the domain of compressed sensing. Furthermore, we review recent advancements in neural network applications for recovery in continuous-time compressed sensing, highlighting the advantages and limitations of this approach.

Real cells and tissues frequently adopt intricate forms that standard mathematical models struggle to replicate. While recent efforts utilize 3D voxel grids and meshes to model extracellular shapes, both formats inherently discretize geometry, which can lead to jagged boundaries. In contrast, treating cell shapes as level sets of Signed Distance Functions (SDFs)—which define boundaries as the zero-level set where distance to the nearest surface is zero—offers a theoretically exact representation while maintaining computational feasibility. Nevertheless, leveraging SDFs for simulation demands innovative techniques, as current models relying on meshes or voxels depend heavily on grid- or cell-based solvers. This work introduces a novel, flexible framework for modeling cell shapes and simulating their physical behaviors, powered by an adaptive multilevel solver. This solver performs finite difference simulations on the grid required to compute the SDF, yet it executes the biological dynamics at the cell's boundary located at the SDF's zero level set. Consequently, this algorithmic shift replaces traditional cell-based solvers with a grid-based solver, significantly shrinking the active computational region. Beyond efficiency gains, this transformation decouples spatial resolution and meshing strategy, allowing shapes and movements defined by global SDFs rather than discrete polygons or voxels, thereby enabling smoother geometries. Furthermore, solving dynamics directly at the interface allows the framework to address various boundary conditions, such as pressure forces and chemotaxis responses, effectively.

This work examines hard-sphere systems through molecular simulations employing the event-chain Monte Carlo (ECMC) algorithm. Unlike the restricted local reversibility found in standard Metropolis algorithms, ECMC facilitates non-reversible, continuous updates, thereby notably accelerating dynamics. Furthermore, it generates ergodic sample space traversals with an efficient rejection rate, producing accurate statistical ensembles. By adapting the ECMC approach for a three-dimensional hard-sphere fluid, we derive improved values for the third and fourth virial coefficients; these exhibit reduced three-dimensional truncation errors owing to accelerated convergence. Our results indicate that third-virial convergence across various fluid densities improves by a factor of four relative to local reversible Metropolis Monte Carlo, while the fourth virial coefficient sees similar gains. Additionally, adapted ECMC yields a $40\%$ enhancement over previous Monte Carlo results for the fluid structure factor across the simple-packed hard-sphere regime. These findings are bolstered by insights from stochastic chemistry theory and results derived from experiments on fluid third virial coefficient values.

Sound Event Detection and Localization (SEDL) and Sound Event Classification (SECC) represent two critical applications in audio signal processing. Both fields benefit significantly from employing convolutional recurrent neural networks (CRNNs) alongside a time-frequency representation channel attention mechanism to enhance performance. This research introduces novel attention strategies to refine existing methods. Specifically, we refine the input configuration using improved auditory convolutional neural networks enhanced with temporal attention modules. Additionally, we develop a refined channel attention mechanism based on adaptive spatial temporal convolution. These advancements are validated across both SEDL and SECC using the crevst-D dataset. Our superior performance relative to baseline techniques underscores the efficacy of integrating advanced attention concepts, temporal convolution, and spatial convolution modules into existing audio analysis frameworks.

Traditional wireless communication relies on separate reception channels, but recent advancements favor simultaneous transmission and reception (STX) architectures that enable dual modes using a single radio frequency (RF) path. While these modes present unique research opportunities, implementing STX with analog-to-digital converters (ADCs) and digital-demodulators in a fully integrated manner remains challenging. To address this, we introduce a novel software-defined superheterodyne receiver (SDSHRH) architecture capable of supporting both conventional and STX operations via a shared front-end, while employing independent direct conversion receivers (RC) for each mode on the same transmission path. Additionally, this work outlines an efficient power amplification scheme designed to minimize self-interference through the utilization of two mutually conjugate matching circuits.

Model Gaussian analytic functions (GAFs) serve as the most prominent examples of stochastic processes defined on complex domains. Unfortunately, their zero sets exhibit properties that significantly hinder rigorous theoretical examination. Grounded in advances within Random Matrix Theory and the emerging field of Random Polynomials, we explore several contemporary challenges regarding the geometry of these zero sets.

This work introduces a novel class of multicluster states within coupled networks of phase oscillators. In these asymmetric clusters, a subset groups maintain near-perpendicular phase differences ($\pi/2$), oscillating as quasi-amplitude oscillators, while the remaining clusters behave approximately as limit oscillators. Our findings indicate that these chimera-like states emerge in lattice configurations with multiple stable fixed-point attractors. Notably, these states persist for extended durations in networks endowed with strong small-world characteristics. Furthermore, we provide a theoretical framework to identify these clusters of amplitude oscillators and verify our results through simulation by utilizing Van der Pol oscillators.

We describe a newly implemented module designed to simulate physical systems with a stochastic influence over particle movement. This module may prove useful for modeling planets and debris disks affected by turbulence. The module allows for the efficient generation of particle-specific correlated noise that conforms with a custom-specified amplitude for the autocorrelation times. The module takes a low footprint in terms of storage memory and can be freely used via the extension effects package in REBOUND-X library.

Quantum theory underpins contemporary science, serving not only as fundamental knowledge but also shaping technological advancements, with feedback control being essential for quantum technologies and numerous industrial applications. A quantum feedback loop comprises measurement and a subsequent classical processing stage. This work examines various measurement strategies and computational techniques within quantum feedback control, addressing both continuous and discontinuous feedback processes from theoretical to practical implementations. Furthermore, it explores applications in quantum thermodynamics, including the quantum Maxwell's demon, and continuous quantum computing, specifically within measurement-based and superconducting architectures, highlighting the quantum Feckel backroad as an exemplary feedback scenario. The paper concludes by outlining specific experimental quantum computing protocols that demonstrate the practical utility of measurement-based quantum feedback control.

Recent numerical investigations by our group (see *Phys. Rev. E* 91, 052102) examined a numerical experiment featuring a narrow channel containing disks with random radii and positions that undergo random, inelastic kicking. Driven particles accumulate at the exits, causing partial or total blockage (jamming). Our analysis, which complements our earlier work on these jammed macrostates, focuses on the phase diagram relative to two control parameters: the inelasticity of flying discs and channel width. Additionally, we present detailed characteristics of the returned joints and the phase transitions themselves.

This study examines historical and projected variations in global seasonal precipitation patterns linked to El Ni\u00f1o-\u00o3-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) events. We utilize a collection of observations, including merged precipitation gauges and reanalyses, alongside a set of 15 multi-model ensembles, both historical and future projections. In our analysis of 107 years of data (1950\u20132047), we detect a "East Pacific" type of ENSO, characterized by the opposing wetting/drying trends, but find no evidence of the "Central Pacific" type during this same period. Projected patterns across 2015\u20142047 reveal a shift toward El Ni\u00f1o of Central Pacific type, with East Pacific type ENSO events still present. Projected precipitation responses to East Pacific type ENSO events are consistently stronger than those associated with the Central Pacific type. We find that current global-scale patterns exhibit a high degree of coherence with long-term global patterns, with model agreement on long-term responses to East Pacific type ENSO events exceeding that to Central Pacific type ENSO events. However, at regional scales, we find that models struggle to capture precipitation changes associated with both types of ENSO events.

Current observations reveal numerous massive black holes (MBHs) in dwarf galaxies situated at significantly lower masses than their counterparts in the Milky Way, challenging standard theoretical models which predict black hole formation only at densities prevalent in larger systems. These "impossible" MBHs are thought to originate from the collapse of ultra-massive Population III stars within the first century of the universe's existence, a scenario that demands specific and distinct observable markers to be verified. In this study, we propose a new signature derived from the MBH formation process in dwarf galaxies, arising from the fragmentation of the hyperbolic outflow generated by the death of these early stars. This debris creates a short-lived, dense cluster following a power-law mass distribution, resembling a "mini-Ultralight Massive Cluster" (Mini-UMC). Such clusters generate gravitational waves (GWs) with micro-hertz frequencies, placing them directly within the detection range of upcoming space-based interferometers, the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA). By analyzing the GW emission from these evolving groups, scientists can investigate properties of Population III remnants and early cosmic structures, offering a novel window into the conditions of the ancient universe.

Electronic flat-band platforms have garnered significant interest recently for their ability to foster diverse quantum phenomena arising from strong electron correlations, such as mini-superconductivity, fractionalization, and topological ordering. Although these effects are theoretically viable, they remain elusive due to the necessity of very low temperatures. This study introduces a model exhibiting a flat band capable of sustaining fractional quantum Hall states at significantly higher filling factors and higher Landau level energies than previously documented scenarios, thereby improving experimental viability. We employ the configuration space nodal method—leveraging its capacity for generating highly entangled wave functions—to conduct variational analyses of the wave function topology, demonstrating the existence of both excitations with fractional charge and $e/4$ quantized Hall conductivity. Additionally, by applying a duality transformation, we identify conditions that produce an effective Hamiltonian resembling the Haldane model, allowing for a transition from an insulating phase to one exhibiting fractional topological order, as further confirmed through mean-field analysis.

We introduce HiPS, a high-performance tool designed for identifying allele-specific open chromatin regions by leveraging Hi-C data and the linkage equilibrium assumption. HPA utilizes all-trans Hi-C profiles to annotate domains with DNAse-I hypersensitive sites and pinpoint allele-specific variants within these regions. Our findings demonstrate that nearly 80% common trait-related SNP loci converge at DNAse-I open chromatin areas detected via HiPS, and the tool exhibits strong correlations with CUT&Tag and CFI-Cseq assays for verifying allele-specific open chromatin. Furthermore, the tool displays robust performance in detecting copy number variation-induced differential chromatin accessibility and integrating methylation data for functional validation. Source code is available at https://github.com/GenomeScienceLab/HiPS.

Consequently, all such designs with point stabilizers forming cyclic groups of prime prime length fall into one of the following categories: the non-trivial primitive groups belong to one of twenty-two known families; otherwise, the design is listed among twelve explicitly named non-trivial examples; or it belongs to one of three non-trivial cases where the point stabilizer is not a cyclic group of prime length.

The dynamics of wide binary (WB) stars offer a vantage point for investigating gravity under the weak acceleration conditions prevalent in a galaxy's periphery. A comprehensive analysis of 37 Wide Binary systems with orbital separations exceeding 100 astronomical units was performed to explore the influence of dark matter subhalos on orbital mechanics. The results indicate that the observed orbital dynamics are consistent with the standard $\Lambda$CDM model combined with standard $N$ point-particle gravity, showing no statistically significant evidence for either modified gravity theories or localized dark matter subhalos. Specifically, the study fails to substantiate the prediction of modified $K$-band gravity regarding a constant orbital velocity for wide binaries. While no specific physical effect was confirmed, the investigation establishes rigorous constraints on both the clustering properties of dark matter and the parameters of modified gravity theories.

We map each multiplicative linear logic proof structure to an ideal of polynomial equations that encapsulates the proof's logical content. Furthermore, this work demonstrates the parallel between the Buchberger algorithm—applied in elimination theories to compute Gr\"obner bases—and the Buchberger-style processes underlying cut-elimination within multiplicative proof nets.

This study introduces a methodology for forecasting the short-term movements of asset price series. By employing pairwise mutual information analysis, the relevant lags between prices and returns were determined. Subsequently, cross-recurrence plot assessments were utilized to pinpoint the most congruent lag values that coincide with minimal complexity and maximal predictability. Ultimately, an integrated lag selection demonstrated that this approach effectively enhances the accuracy of short-term forecasting.

Terahertz radiation enables the selective tuning of vibrations within molecules and crystal lattices, revealing how the circular paths taken by ions generate inertial influences on electrons that parallel the classical concepts of Coriolis and centrifugal forces. Consequently, controlling directionally circular movements of ions offers a method to manipulate the electronic properties of condensed matter through THz exposure.

This paper introduces CTRPlus, a new click-through rate prediction framework designed to enhance existing models by integrating external knowledge specifically beneficial for novel advertisements lacking sufficient historical data. Drawing inspiration from the cross-attention mechanism within Transformer architectures, the system learns the alignment between internal representation features and external knowledge graph nodes. By integrating this external knowledge layer into standard deep learning ad prediction pipelines, a unique learning signal is established to boost cold-start performance. Comprehensive evaluations conducted across two large-scale industrial datasets confirm that the proposed model surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, the study emphasizes the substantial benefit derived from incorporating cold-start strategies targeted at new items.

Historically, business process management has focused on rigid, step-by-workflows. In reality, however, numerous knowledge-intensive processes contain both structured and semi-structured components. This paper introduces a modeling approach utilizing Petri nets capable of representing interactions within knowledge pools, workflow pools, and structured and semi-structured activity pools. We specifically extract structured and semi-structured activity pools from free-form petri nets through the application of formal criteria. This formulation enables the formulation structured activity rules without breaking the petri net's free-form nature, thus preserving its capacity to model concurrency, resource constraints, and state-dependent logic. We demonstrate that these petri nets composed of different activity pools can be mapped to this notation through a one-to-one correspondence, maintaining mathematical equivalence. This equivalence facilitates more effective model verification while supporting dynamic behavior modeling necessary for complex processes.

Wildfire atmospheric plumes often travel vast distances, settling aerosols that degrade outdoor visibility and solar energy output, thereby solar panel performance. This study examines how such aerosols impact solar generation, using data from California panels during 2017 fires. By leveraging localized concentration estimates and inverter smart-meter readings, the work quantifies aerosol deposition effects and technical solar yield losses. The results reveal substantial production declines, suggesting that conventional cleaning regimes may under-maintenance panels. These findings offer utility operators and inverters practical insights for optimizing washing schedules, showcasing how atmospheric events directly translate into economic solar losses and potential system optimization needs.

Offering meaningful privacy protection for users of location-based systems is exceptionally difficult when multiple nearby positions are reported in rapid succession, as this implies valuable insights into their daily habits. Current anonymization techniques, predominantly rooted in spatial offsetting and zone partitioning, often fail to provide adequate safeguarding under these conditions. This paper introduces a rigorous mathematical framework tailored specifically for this scenario and utilizes it to evaluate the efficacy of prevalent methods such as generalized spatial offsetting, zone-based approaches, clustering, releasing fictitious data points, and proposed new techniques. Our comprehensive analysis considers both the extent of information concealed and the degree of inconvenience imposed upon users. Extensive experiments conducted across three real-world datasets reveal that current generalized forms of spatial offsetting are fundamentally flawed in this context. Conversely, two original methods designed by our team successfully achieve a balance between private preservation and user utility.

Resting-state fMRI research is increasingly pursuing multisite designs to expedite recruitment and lower expenses; however, technical variations across scanning machines often introduce site-specific effects that complicate data integration. While preprocessing attempts to mitigate these issues, their complete elimination remains unverified. This study applies linear mixed-effects models to multisite functional fMRI data from 565 participants across four locations, evaluating connectivity within the default mode network. By contrasting results from repeated-measures ANOVA, linear mixed-effects models, and site-effect-corrected data, we examine the impact of these variations on statistical power to distinguish between two groups. Our findings confirm that anatomical scanning discrepancies are pervasive and significantly impair a standard ANOVA approach at the multisite level. In contrast, incorporating site as a random variable in a linear mixed-effects model yields group effect estimates and detection power nearly equivalent to those from ANOVA. Nevertheless, we observe a slight reduction in power when using the mixed-effects framework due to reduced sample sizes for the between-subjects effect, a disadvantage that worsens as the number of sites increases. Crucially, for small cohort sizes typical of many fMRI studies, biasing caused by uncontrolled site effects in ANOVA exceeds the minor power loss associated with mixed-effects modeling, making the latter the preferable strategy.

In prior research, the authors presented a Lin-Lu-Yau style Ricci curvature for directed graphs, aligned with the Chung Laplacian framework. The goal of this paper is to establish a characterization akin to that of von Renesse and Sturm, demonstrating our lower Ricci curvature bound through a heat semigroup's gradient estimate and a corresponding transportation inequality during heat diffusion. A key outcome of this effort is proving a concentration of measure result for directed graphs exhibiting positive Ricci curvature.

Recently, Natural Language Processing for Code-Swapper (CM) texts has seen advancements largely driven by word-formation models trained on single-language (monolingual) datasets. Although these word-form features often yield superior performance than plaintext tokens, the current body of research lacks comprehensive studies on creating background embeddings specifically for multi-lingual (codex-mix) languages. This paper introduces a self-formation model tailored to create word-form features and background embeddings codex-mix data. The proposed method includes separate layers for each specific language found in codex-mix text. To validate the approach, the authors present the development of a Codex-Mix-BERT based on multilingual pre-trained weights and the encoded San-Sanskrit (Hindi-Urdus) codex-mix dataset. Empirical results indicate that our proposed method surpasses in performance models with input of plaintext tokens, confirming the superior efficacy of our word-formation architecture.
